```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, fig.retina = 2, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
has_stan <- requireNamespace("cmdstanr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  !is.null(tryCatch(cmdstanr::cmdstan_path(), error = function(e) NULL))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_stan)
cols <- c(blue = "#4F6D8F", red = "#C8553D", gold = "#E0A458", grey = "#8C8C8C")
```

Comparative data are rarely one clean value per species. A species may be
represented by several records, such as population means from different
studies, each with its own standard error. Some species in the tree may
have no data at all. This vignette works through three examples:

* **records with known standard errors**: several records per species,
  each with its own measurement error, separated from true variation
  within species;
* **an evolving slope with individual data**: a regression slope that
  evolves along the tree, estimated from records rather than species
  means;
* **predicting species without data** under kernels with latent values,
  such as `k_relaxed()`, where the prediction has to account for the rate
  on the new species' own branch.

Each example simulates its own data, so the true values are known. All
models are fitted with Stan, so the vignette needs `cmdstanr` and CmdStan.
The article "What works with what" on the package website lists which
kernels combine with which features.

```{r tree}
library(phylogp)
set.seed(13)
tr <- ape::rphylo(100, birth = 1, death = 0)              # a pure-birth tree
tr$edge.length <- tr$edge.length / max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tr))  # height 1
N <- ape::Ntip(tr)
```

## Records with known standard errors

Suppose each record is a population mean taken from the literature, based
on a few to a few dozen specimens, and reported with its standard error.
A species has one to five such records. Records of a species differ for
two reasons: real differences among populations (variation within the
species) and sampling error, which the standard errors describe. Both are
added to the variance of a record:

$$y_{ij} = \mu_i + e_{ij}, \qquad e_{ij} \sim N(0,\ \sigma_w^2 + \mathrm{se}_{ij}^2),$$

where $\mu_i$ is the species value, given by the kernel, and $\sigma_w$ is
`within_sigma`. Records with small standard errors count for more. The
likelihood is exact and stays linear in the number of species.

We simulate species values from Brownian motion plus a non-phylogenetic
species effect, variation among populations with standard deviation
0.15, and standard errors from $0.8 / \sqrt{n}$ for $n$ specimens.

```{r records-data}
set.seed(1)
mu <- kernel_simulate(k_bm() + k_white(), tr,
                      pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 1), white1 = list(sigma = 0.2)))[, 1]
rec <- data.frame(species = rep(tr$tip.label, sample(1:5, N, replace = TRUE)))
rec$n  <- sample(3:40, nrow(rec), replace = TRUE)          # specimens per record
rec$se <- 0.8 / sqrt(rec$n)
rec$y  <- 1 + mu[rec$species] + rnorm(nrow(rec), 0, 0.15) + rnorm(nrow(rec), 0, rec$se)
nrow(rec)
summary(rec$se)
```

We fit the model twice, once with the standard errors (`se = "se"`) and
once without them.

```{r records-fit}
f_se   <- phylo_gp(y ~ 1, rec, tr, k_bm() + k_white(),
                   species = "species", se = "se", seed = 1)
f_nose <- phylo_gp(y ~ 1, rec, tr, k_bm() + k_white(),
                   species = "species", seed = 1)
f_se
```

The model without standard errors has no way to tell sampling error from
real differences among populations, so it puts both into `within_sigma`:

```{r records-compare}
pick <- function(f) summary(f)[summary(f)$parameter == "within_sigma", c("mean", "q5", "q95")]
rbind("with se" = pick(f_se), "without se" = pick(f_nose), truth = c(0.15, NA, NA))
```

With the standard errors, `within_sigma` is close to the true 0.15.
Without them it is nearly twice the true value, and it then describes the
quality of the records as much as the biology. The difference matters
when `within_sigma` is itself of interest, for example when comparing
variation within species to variation among them, and it also changes how
much each record counts: without standard errors, a record from three
specimens counts as much as one from forty.

`predict()` works as for any other fit. For a fit with several rows per
species, `newdata` names species in the same column as the data, and
`type = "response"` predicts a new record, including `within_sigma` (a new
record's own standard error is not known, so it is not added).

## An evolving slope with individual data

`k_slope("body") * k_bm()` gives a regression slope that evolves along the
tree as Brownian motion: each species has its own slope, and related
species have similar ones [@hadfield2010]. With several records per
species, each record contributes its own predictor value, so the slope of
a species is informed both by where the species sits relative to others
and by the variation among its own records.

We simulate body size for each species, three to eight individuals per
species around it, and a brain–body slope whose deviation from 0.7
evolves along the tree.

```{r slope-data}
set.seed(5)
body_sp   <- kernel_simulate(k_bm(), tr, pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 1.5)))[, 1]
slope_dev <- kernel_simulate(k_bm(), tr, pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 0.5)))[, 1]
resid_sp  <- kernel_simulate(k_bm() + k_white(), tr,
                             pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 0.5), white1 = list(sigma = 0.1)))[, 1]
ind <- data.frame(species = rep(tr$tip.label, sample(3:8, N, replace = TRUE)))
ind$body <- body_sp[ind$species] + rnorm(nrow(ind), 0, 0.4)
centre <- mean(ind$body)
ind$brain <- 0.5 + (0.7 + slope_dev[ind$species]) * (ind$body - centre) +
  resid_sp[ind$species] + rnorm(nrow(ind), 0, 0.2)
true_slope <- 0.7 + slope_dev
nrow(ind)
```

We compare a constant slope with a slope that evolves along the tree.
`body` is centred at its mean over all records, the reference point for
the slope deviations.

```{r slope-fit}
f_const <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, ind, tr, k_bm() + k_white(),
                    species = "species", seed = 1)
f_vary  <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, ind, tr,
                    k_bm() + k_slope("body") * k_bm() + k_white(),
                    species = "species", seed = 1)
loo::loo_compare(list("constant slope" = loo(f_const),
                      "evolving slope" = loo(f_vary)))
```

Leave-one-out leaves out a whole species, all its records at once, so the
comparison asks how well each model predicts a species it has not seen.
The evolving slope wins clearly. A few species are flagged with Pareto
$\hat k > 0.7$; in a real analysis, `loo_refit()` recomputes their
contributions exactly (see `vignette("slopes-prediction", package =
"phylogp")`). `varying_slopes()` returns the posterior slope of every
species and node:

```{r slope-recovery, fig.height = 4.6}
vs <- varying_slopes(f_vary)
tips <- vs[!is.na(vs$label), ]
truth <- true_slope[tips$label]

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 3, 1))
ft <- f_vary$tree
plot_tree_values(ft, vs$mean[ft$edge[, 2]], center = 0.7, lim = 1,
                 main = "Estimated slope (posterior mean)")
plot(truth, tips$mean, type = "n", las = 1, bty = "l",
     ylim = range(tips$q5, tips$q95), xlab = "true slope",
     ylab = "estimated slope (90% interval)", main = "Species", font.main = 1)
segments(truth, tips$q5, y1 = tips$q95, col = adjustcolor(cols["blue"], 0.35), lwd = 2)
points(truth, tips$mean, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, col = cols["blue"])
abline(0, 1, col = cols["red"], lwd = 1.5)
par(op)
c(correlation = cor(truth, tips$mean),
  coverage_90 = mean(tips$q5 < truth & truth < tips$q95))
```

The slopes along the tree are recovered well. Each species contributes
several body sizes, so its own records inform its slope, not only its
relatives. Species with extreme slopes in clades whose other members have
ordinary ones are still shrunk towards their relatives, as for the two
points at the right. Standard errors per
record (`se`) can be added to this model in the same way as above.

## Predicting species without data under variable rates

Predicting a species that is in the tree but has no data is kriging on the
tree [@garland2000]: the species is predicted from its relatives through
the kernel. Under Brownian motion the kernel is fixed once its parameters
are. Under `k_relaxed()` the rate of evolution varies along the tree, and
the rate on the branch leading to a new species was never fitted, because
that branch was not in the fitted tree. `predict()` draws it, for each
posterior draw, from its distribution given the fitted rates: a Brownian
bridge along the fitted branch that the new species joins, and Brownian
motion along its own branch. A species that joins a fast-evolving clade
therefore inherits a high rate, and with it a wider prediction interval.

We simulate a clade of about 20 species whose trait evolves 8 times faster
than elsewhere, as in `vignette("phylogp", package = "phylogp")`.

```{r fast-clade}
clade_sizes <- lengths(ape::prop.part(tr))
fast_node <- N + which.min(abs(clade_sizes - 20))
descendants <- function(node) {
  kids <- tr$edge[tr$edge[, 1] == node, 2]
  c(node, unlist(lapply(kids, descendants)))
}
in_clade <- descendants(fast_node)
fast_tips <- tr$tip.label[intersect(in_clade, seq_len(N))]

set.seed(7)
z <- numeric(N + tr$Nnode)
z[in_clade] <- log(8)
body  <- kernel_simulate(k_bm(), tr, pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 1.5)))[, 1]
resid <- kernel_simulate(k_relaxed() + k_white(), tr,
                         pars = list(relaxed1 = list(sigma = 1, z = z),
                                     white1   = list(sigma = 0.1)))[, 1]
d <- data.frame(body = body, brain = 0.5 + 0.7 * body + resid[names(body)])
```

We hold out six species in the fast clade and six elsewhere, fit Brownian
motion and the relaxed-rate kernel to the remaining 88, and predict the
twelve held-out species from their body sizes and positions in the tree.

```{r predict-fit}
set.seed(3)
held <- c(sample(fast_tips, 6), sample(setdiff(tr$tip.label, fast_tips), 6))
train <- d[setdiff(rownames(d), held), ]
f_bm      <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, train, tr, k_bm() + k_white(), seed = 1)
f_relaxed <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, train, tr, k_relaxed() + k_white(), seed = 1)

p_bm      <- predict(f_bm, newdata = d[held, ], tree = tr)
p_relaxed <- predict(f_relaxed, newdata = d[held, ], tree = tr)
```

The fits only contain the 88 training species; `tree = tr` supplies the
full tree, so `predict()` knows where the held-out species attach.

```{r predict-plot, fig.height = 4.4}
p <- rbind(cbind(p_bm, model = "BM"), cbind(p_relaxed, model = "relaxed"))
p$truth <- d[p$species, "brain"]
p$fast  <- p$species %in% fast_tips
ord <- held[order(!held %in% fast_tips, d[held, "brain"])]
x <- match(p$species, ord) + ifelse(p$model == "BM", -0.15, 0.15)
mcol <- ifelse(p$model == "BM", cols["grey"], cols["blue"])

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(x, p$mean, type = "n", las = 1, bty = "l", xaxt = "n",
     ylim = range(p$q5, p$q95, p$truth), xlab = "", ylab = "log brain size")
rect(0.5, par("usr")[3], 6.5, par("usr")[4], col = adjustcolor(cols["gold"], 0.15), border = NA)
segments(x, p$q5, y1 = p$q95, col = adjustcolor(mcol, 0.7), lwd = 4)
points(x, p$mean, pch = 19, col = mcol)
points(seq_along(ord), d[ord, "brain"], pch = 4, lwd = 2, col = cols["red"])
axis(1, at = c(3.5, 9.5), labels = c("fast clade", "other species"), tick = FALSE)
legend("bottomright", c("BM (90% interval)", "relaxed (90% interval)", "true value"),
       pch = c(19, 19, 4), col = cols[c("grey", "blue", "red")], lwd = c(NA, NA, 2),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
par(op)
```

```{r predict-summary}
p$width <- p$q95 - p$q5
p$covered <- p$q5 < p$truth & p$truth < p$q95
aggregate(cbind(width, covered) ~ model + fast, data = p, FUN = mean)
```

Brownian motion fits one rate to the whole tree, a compromise between the
fast clade and the rest, so its intervals have about the same width
everywhere. The relaxed-rate kernel makes them wider in the fast clade and
narrower elsewhere. With twelve species the difference is modest, and
both models miss the same species in the fast clade, but the direction is
the one expected: the relaxed kernel's uncertainty follows the rate of
evolution where the species sits. The point estimates hardly differ,
because both models predict a species mainly from its closest relatives.

The same holds for the other kernels with latent values. Under
`k_rate_time()` a new species uses the fitted rates of the time intervals
its branch spans. Under Student-t residuals, `k_white(df = 4)`, a new
species' variance multiplier is drawn from its prior, so its predictive
distribution has heavier tails than a Gaussian. Under
`k_slope("body") * k_bm()` its slope deviation is drawn along its branch,
as for relaxed rates, so its prediction uses a slope close to those of its
relatives.
